gapFill.title: Fill in the gaps
gapFill.subtitle: Type a or an. If the sentence needs no article, type — (a dash). Twenty original sentences.

questions.explain: ‘Dream’ is singular and countable, and it is new information. ‘Strange’ starts with a consonant sound, so we say ‘a strange dream’.
‘Dolphins’ is plural, so there is no a/an. Leave the gap empty (—) or use ‘some’.
‘Old’ starts with a vowel sound (/əʊ/), so we say ‘an old church’.

questions.after: nurse at a hospital in Girona.
questions.explain: A job is a singular countable noun, so it takes a/an. ‘Nurse’ starts with a consonant sound: ‘a nurse’.
After ‘what’, a singular noun takes a/an. ‘Amazing’ starts with a vowel sound: ‘what an amazing goal’.
Here ‘a’ means ‘per’ (every): ‘twice a week’. ‘Twice per week’ is also correct.
‘Eyes’ is plural, so there is no a/an: ‘green eyes’.

questions.before: When he grows up, he wants to be
questions.explain: A job takes a/an. ‘Architect’ starts with a vowel sound (/ɑː/): ‘an architect’.
‘Bank’ is singular and countable, and we are asking about any bank, not a particular one: ‘a bank’.

questions.before: The car was going at 100 kilometres
questions.explain: ‘Hour’ starts with a silent h, so it begins with a vowel sound: ‘an hour’. Here ‘an’ means ‘per’; ‘per hour’ is also correct.
‘Advice’ is uncountable, so it can’t take a/an: ‘good advice’ or ‘some good advice’.
‘Brother’ is a singular countable noun and this is new information. ‘Younger’ starts with a consonant sound (/j/): ‘a younger brother’.

questions.before: Once upon a time, there was
questions.explain: A story introduces a new character, so we use a/an. ‘Ugly’ starts with a vowel sound (/ʌ/): ‘an ugly dragon’.
Here ‘a’ means ‘one’: ‘a minute’ = one minute (‘one minute’ is also correct). ‘Minute’ starts with a consonant sound.
‘News’ looks plural but is uncountable, so it can’t take a/an: ‘good news’ or ‘some good news’.
We say ‘a friend of mine’ (one of my friends). We don’t put ‘a’ before ‘my’.
A new person, so a/an. ‘Interesting’ starts with a vowel sound (/ɪ/): ‘an interesting woman’.
‘Milk’ is uncountable here, so there is no a/an. ‘Some milk’ and ‘any milk’ are also fine in this question.
After ‘works as’, a singular job takes a/an. ‘Chef’ starts with a consonant sound (/ʃ/): ‘a chef’.
‘Rainbow’ is singular and countable and we are seeing it for the first time: ‘a rainbow’.

wordOrder.title: Put it in order
wordOrder.subtitle: Tap the words to build each sentence — 20 examples with a, an and some.

matching.title: Why a / an?
matching.subtitle: Tap a sentence, then tap the use that matches it.

pairs.left: My mum is a dentist.
I saw a fox in the garden.
I go to the gym three times a week.
What a lovely surprise!
He’s an electrician.
There’s a new shop on my street.
Bananas are one euro a kilo.
What an ugly dog!
I want to be a vet.
We met a strange man at the station.
He drives at 50 miles an hour.
What a mess!
My brother is a firefighter.
Is there a pharmacy near here?
I brush my teeth twice a day.
What an amazing goal!
She works as an engineer.

The tickets cost ten euros a person.
What a great idea!

timedMC.title: Beat the clock
timedMC.subtitle: 15 seconds per question. Singular countable noun → a / an. Plural or uncountable → no a / an.

questions.text: Yesterday I met        interesting woman on the train.
wrongReasons: ‘Interesting’ starts with a vowel sound (/ɪ/), so ‘a’ doesn’t fit.
‘Woman’ is singular and countable, so it needs a/an.
questions.explain: A new person, and ‘interesting’ starts with a vowel sound: an interesting woman.

questions.text: My brother is        police officer.
wrongReasons: ‘Police’ starts with a consonant sound (/p/), so ‘an’ doesn’t fit.
A singular job needs a/an: ‘a police officer’.
questions.explain: A job takes a/an, and ‘police’ starts with a consonant sound: a police officer.

questions.text: She works as        engineer for a big company.
wrongReasons: ‘Engineer’ starts with a vowel sound (/e/), so we need ‘an’.
After ‘works as’, a singular job takes a/an.
questions.explain: ‘Works as’ + job, and ‘engineer’ starts with a vowel sound: as an engineer.

questions.text: I bought        apples at the market.
wrongReasons: ‘Apples’ is plural, so ‘an’ can’t go before it.
‘Apples’ is plural, so ‘a’ can’t go before it.
‘One’ goes with a singular noun: ‘one apple’, not ‘one apples’.
questions.explain: A plural noun takes no a/an: ‘I bought apples’ (or ‘some apples’).

questions.text: Can you give me        advice, please?
wrongReasons: ‘Advice’ is uncountable, so it can’t take ‘an’.
‘Advice’ is uncountable, so it can’t take ‘a’.
‘One advice’ doesn’t work; to count it, say ‘a piece of advice’.
questions.explain: Uncountable nouns take ‘some’ instead of a/an: some advice.

questions.text: I see my grandparents once        month.
wrongReasons: ‘Once the month’ is a common slip; to mean ‘per’ we use ‘a’: once a month.
‘Month’ starts with a consonant sound (/m/), so ‘an’ doesn’t fit.
‘Once month’ is missing the article that means ‘per’.
questions.explain: ‘A’ means ‘per’ (every): once a month.

questions.text: What        terrible film!
wrongReasons: ‘Terrible’ starts with a consonant sound (/t/), so ‘an’ doesn’t fit.
In an exclamation with a singular noun we say ‘what a/an’, not ‘what the’.
A singular countable noun after ‘what’ needs a/an.
questions.explain: What + a + adjective + singular noun: What a terrible film!

questions.text: What        lovely weather!
wrongReasons: ‘Weather’ is uncountable, so it can’t take ‘a’.
‘Weather’ is uncountable, so it can’t take ‘an’.
‘What the lovely weather!’ isn’t how we make this exclamation; an uncountable noun takes no article.
questions.explain: With an uncountable noun there is no article: What lovely weather!

questions.text: There’s        message for you on the desk.
wrongReasons: ‘Message’ starts with a consonant sound (/m/), so ‘an’ doesn’t fit.
‘There’s the message’ would mean we both know which message; this is the first mention.
‘Message’ is singular and countable, so it needs a/an.
questions.explain: First mention of a singular countable noun: a message.

questions.text: I’m looking for        umbrella; mine is broken.
wrongReasons: ‘Umbrella’ starts with a vowel sound (/ʌ/), so we need ‘an’.
‘Umbrella’ is singular and countable, so it needs a/an.
questions.explain: Any umbrella, not a particular one, and a vowel sound: an umbrella.

questions.text: Shakespeare was        English writer.
wrongReasons: ‘English’ starts with a vowel sound (/ɪ/), so we need ‘an’.
‘Writer’ is singular and countable, so it needs an article.
questions.explain: One of many English writers, and ‘English’ starts with a vowel sound: an English writer.

questions.text: We need        furniture for the new flat.
wrongReasons: ‘Furniture’ is uncountable, so it can’t take ‘a’.
‘Furniture’ is uncountable, so it can’t take ‘an’.
‘One furniture’ doesn’t work; to count it, say ‘a piece of furniture’.
questions.explain: Uncountable noun: some furniture.

questions.text: He’s        old friend of mine.
wrongReasons: ‘Old’ starts with a vowel sound (/əʊ/), so we need ‘an’.
‘He’s my old friend of mine’ repeats the possessive; say ‘my old friend’ or ‘an old friend of mine’.
questions.explain: a/an + noun + of + mine: an old friend of mine.

questions.text: The speed limit here is thirty miles        hour.
wrongReasons: ‘Hour’ has a silent h, so it starts with a vowel sound: ‘an hour’.
‘Thirty miles the hour’ is a common slip; ‘an’ means ‘per’.
Without an article it doesn’t mean ‘per hour’.
questions.explain: ‘An’ means ‘per’, and the silent h gives a vowel sound: an hour.

questions.text: Is your sister        student?
wrongReasons: ‘Student’ starts with a consonant sound (/s/), so ‘an’ doesn’t fit.
A singular role needs a/an: ‘a student’.
questions.explain: A role takes a/an: a student.

questions.text: They are        doctors.
wrongReasons: ‘Doctors’ is plural, so ‘a’ can’t go before it.
‘Doctors’ is plural, so ‘an’ can’t go before it.
‘One’ goes with a singular noun: ‘one doctor’.
questions.explain: Plural jobs take no a/an: They are doctors.

questions.text: Which sentence is correct?
wrongReasons: A singular job needs a/an: ‘an actress’.
‘Actress’ starts with a vowel sound (/æ/), so we need ‘an’.
questions.explain: A job takes a/an, and ‘actress’ starts with a vowel sound: an actress.

questions.text: Which sentence is correct?
wrongReasons: ‘Homework’ is uncountable, so it can’t take ‘a’.
‘Many’ is for countable nouns. ‘Homework’ is uncountable, so use ‘some homework’.
‘One homework’ doesn’t work; to count it, say ‘a piece of homework’.
questions.explain: Uncountable noun: some homework.

questions.text: We had        honest conversation about it.
wrongReasons: ‘Honest’ starts with a silent h, so it begins with a vowel sound: ‘an honest’.
‘Conversation’ is singular and countable, so it needs a/an.
questions.explain: Silent h gives a vowel sound: an honest conversation.

questions.text: She wants to study at        university in Scotland.
wrongReasons: ‘University’ starts with /j/ (like ‘you’), which is a consonant sound, so ‘an’ doesn’t fit.
‘University’ is singular and countable, so it needs a/an.
questions.explain: /j/ is a consonant sound: a university.

errorCorrection.title: Find the mistake
errorCorrection.subtitle: Each sentence has exactly one mistake. Tap the word you think is wrong (if a word is missing, tap the word right after the gap). Twenty original sentences.

items.message: ‘Teacher’ starts with a consonant sound (/t/), so we say ‘a teacher’, not ‘an teacher’.
A job is a singular countable noun, so it needs a/an: ‘She is a nurse’.
‘Hour’ has a silent h, so it starts with a vowel sound: ‘an hour’.
‘University’ starts with /j/ (like ‘you’), a consonant sound, so we say ‘a university’.
‘Umbrella’ starts with a vowel sound (/ʌ/), so we say ‘an umbrella’.
‘Honest’ starts with a silent h, so it begins with a vowel sound: ‘an honest man’.
‘Amazing’ starts with a vowel sound, so the exclamation is ‘What an amazing view!’.
‘Advice’ is uncountable, so it can’t take a/an: say ‘some advice’ or ‘a piece of advice’.
‘Information’ is uncountable, so it can’t take a/an: ‘some information’ or ‘a piece of information’.
‘News’ looks plural but is uncountable, so it can’t take a/an: ‘some good news’ or ‘a piece of good news’.
‘Homework’ is uncountable, so it can’t take ‘a’: say ‘some homework’.
‘Eyes’ is plural, so there is no ‘a’ before ‘blue eyes’.
‘Shoes’ is plural, so there is no ‘a’: ‘new shoes’ (or ‘a pair of new shoes’).
To say ‘per’ (every) we use ‘a’, not ‘the’: ‘twice a week’.
‘A’ means ‘per’ in prices: ‘two euros a kilo’, not ‘the kilo’.
After ‘what’, a singular countable noun needs a/an: ‘What a lovely surprise!’.
We don’t use ‘a’ before ‘my’: say ‘my friend’ or ‘a friend of mine’.
‘Fox’ is singular and countable, so it needs a/an when we mention it for the first time: ‘a fox’.
A job is a singular countable noun, so it needs a/an: ‘a vet’.
‘Elephant’ starts with a vowel sound (/e/), so we say ‘an elephant’.

levelCheck.title: How well do you know it?
levelCheck.subtitle: 20 mixed questions — typing, word order, which rule, multiple choice and spot-the-mistake. In the typing questions write a or an, or — (a dash) if no article is needed. One pass, then a breakdown of where you’re strong and where to go back and practise.

items.sentText: My aunt is {{blank}} lawyer in Barcelona.
items.explain: A job is a singular countable noun, so it needs a/an. ‘Lawyer’ starts with a consonant sound: ‘a lawyer’.
items.wrongNote: ‘Lawyer’ starts with a consonant sound, so ‘a’.

items.explain: ‘An’ means ‘per’ here, and the silent h gives a vowel sound: ‘an hour’ (‘per hour’ is also correct).
items.wrongNote: ‘Hour’ has a silent h, so use ‘an’.

items.sentText: Could you give me {{blank}} help with this exercise?
items.explain: ‘Help’ is uncountable here, so there is no a/an: ‘some help’, or just ‘help’.
items.wrongNote: ‘Help’ is uncountable, so it takes no a/an.

items.sentText: I found {{blank}} old photo in a box.
items.explain: A new thing, and ‘old’ starts with a vowel sound: ‘an old photo’.
items.wrongNote: ‘Old’ starts with a vowel sound, so use ‘an’.

wrongReasons: ‘Dentist’ isn’t a unit of time, speed or price, so ‘a’ doesn’t mean ‘per’.
There’s no ‘what’, so it isn’t an exclamation.
We are saying what her job is, not introducing a new thing.
items.explain: ‘A’ before a job says what someone is.

items.text: In ‘three times a day’, what does ‘a’ mean?
wrongReasons: ‘Day’ is a unit of time here, not a new thing we are introducing.
‘Day’ isn’t a job.
There’s no ‘what’, so it isn’t an exclamation.
items.explain: ‘A’ means ‘per’ with time, speed and price: three times a day.

items.text: Why is there no a/an in ‘She has green eyes’?
wrongReasons: ‘Eyes’ can be counted (one eye, two eyes), so it isn’t uncountable.
‘Eyes’ isn’t a job.
There’s no ‘what’, so it isn’t an exclamation.
‘Noise’ is singular here, so it isn’t plural.
‘Noise’ isn’t a job.
There’s no time, speed or price, so ‘an’ doesn’t mean ‘per’.
items.explain: ‘Awful’ starts with a vowel sound, so we say ‘an awful noise’.

items.text: We saw {{blank}} elephants at the safari park.
wrongReasons: ‘Elephants’ is plural, so ‘an’ can’t go before it.
‘Elephants’ is plural, so ‘a’ can’t go before it.
‘One’ goes with a singular noun: ‘one elephant’.
items.explain: A plural noun takes no a/an.

wrongReasons: ‘Interesting’ starts with a vowel sound (/ɪ/), so ‘a’ doesn’t fit.
In an exclamation with a singular noun we say ‘what a/an’, not ‘what the’.
A singular countable noun after ‘what’ needs a/an.
items.explain: ‘Interesting’ starts with a vowel sound: What an interesting idea!

wrongReasons: ‘Information’ is uncountable, so it can’t take ‘an’.
‘Information’ is uncountable, so it can’t take ‘a’.
‘One information’ doesn’t work; to count it, say ‘a piece of information’.
‘Actor’ starts with a vowel sound (/æ/), so we need ‘an’.
A singular job needs a/an.
items.explain: A job takes a/an, and ‘actor’ starts with a vowel sound: an actor.

items.message: A job is a singular countable noun, so it needs a/an: ‘a pilot’.
‘Help’ is uncountable, so it can’t take ‘a’: say ‘some help’.
‘A’ means ‘per’ here, so we need it: ‘three times a day’.
‘Teachers’ is plural, so there is no ‘a’: ‘My parents are teachers’.
